title: Maintenance Fabric for Predictable Throughput During Node Lifecycle
creator: Asha Patel
description: Introduce a lightweight fleet-level 'maintenance fabric' that coordinates node lifecycle operations (drain, upgrade, reprovision) with throughput reservation tokens, autoscaler surge policies, and KV-cache warmup to keep customer-facing throughput within contractual guarantees. This ticket scopes the MVP runtime + control-plane contract, operational runbook, and a small console surface for on-call awareness.
acceptance_criteria: Control plane can issue throughput reservation tokens for a maintenance window and assign them to in-flight drains.
Autoscaler can temporarily allocate surge capacity controlled by policy and release it automatically when drain completes.
KV-cache warmup hooks are invoked for target hosts before traffic shift to avoid cold-cache tail latencies.
SLO indicators (p50/p95 latency and tokens/sec) remain within defined degradation thresholds during a staged 10-node rolling upgrade in a dedicated pool.
Console shows per-maintenance-window view with reservation status, progress, and links to diagnostics.
Runbook added to Confluence with rollback and emergency stop procedures and validated by on-call drills.
design_decisions: Use tokenized throughput reservations (soft guarantees) instead of hard capacity pinning to preserve cluster bin-packing and reduce wasted resources.
Integrate with existing autoscaler API via a short-lived surge lease rather than expanding long-term reserved capacity.
KV-cache warmup will be opt-in per fleet with a small HTTP hook on runtime; avoids mandatory runtime changes for fleets that don't use KV-cache.
Maintenance windows are expressed as time ranges + reservation token budget; rollouts split into micro-slices (default 20% of budget per slice).
Expose telemetry via existing route-level dashboards instead of building a new UI backend.
Fallback policy: if reserve tokens exhausted, degrade to lower-throughput model variant and notify on-call.
rollout_plan: Feature-flagged control-plane rollout in staging (week 1): create and consume reservation tokens in a small test pool.
Runtime integration (week 2): add KV-cache warmup hook and autoscaler surge lease handling behind feature flags.
Canary in production (week 3): enable for a single dedicated customer pool with on-call support and extended monitoring.
Gradual expansion (weeks 4-6): incrementally enable on fleets with explicit opt-in; collect SLO regressions and cost metrics.
Full opt-in GA (week 8): document runbook, console surface, and billing considerations for reservation token consumption.
metrics: Maintenance window P95 latency delta compared to baseline
KV-cache hit rate change during and after warmup
risks: Over-provisioning during surge leases could increase costs; need conservative default surge sizes and cost alerts.
KV-cache warmup hook could introduce slowdowns if misused; require timeouts and rate limits on warmup calls.
Coordination bugs between control-plane token state and runtime may lead to stuck drains; mitigation: idempotent state machine and observability traces.
Customers may expect hard guarantees; documentation must be explicit that tokens are soft and subject to capacity constraints.
